title: Kindred
intro: Nine images about the human side of our earliest ancestors. Not the hunt, but the qualities that kept them alive: love, family, care, art, music, friendship, teamwork, and endurance. Two bands, one on the coast of southern Africa and one in Ice Age Europe, tens of thousands of years ago.
style: In the spirit of Joseph Wright of Derby

images.title: The Hearth
images.description_1: At dusk in a rock shelter above the sea, an elder tells the band a story by the fire. A child sits close, and red handprints mark the wall behind them. Before writing, the stories lived in the people.
images.description_2: In Blombos Cave, on the coast of South Africa, people engraved crosshatch patterns on pieces of red ochre more than 70,000 years ago. These are some of the oldest known designs made by human hands.
images.alt: Oil painting of a band of early humans in hide cloaks and shell beads sitting around a fire in a sandstone rock shelter, facing a white-bearded elder who tells a story, with a small child near the fire, red handprints on the wall, and a sunset sea through the shelter mouth.

images.title: The Flute
images.description_1: Snow falls outside a cave in Ice Age Europe. Inside, a father plays a flute carved from bird bone, and his family turns toward the music. Horses painted in red ochre and charcoal run along the wall behind them.
images.description_2: In caves in southern Germany, archaeologists found flutes made from the wing bones of vultures and swans. They are about 40,000 years old, the oldest known musical instruments in the world.
images.alt: Oil painting of an Ice Age family in fur parkas around a fire in a cave mouth, a man playing a small bone flute, a woman holding a baby, horse paintings on the firelit wall, and a moonlit frozen valley outside.

images.title: Love
images.description_1: At the edge of the sea, two people string a necklace of shells together, their hands joined over the beads.
images.description_2: In Blombos Cave, archaeologists found small shells, each pierced with one hole, about 75,000 years old. Wear marks around the holes show that they hung on a cord for a long time. Someone collected them, pierced them, and wore them, or gave them to someone else.
images.alt: Oil painting of an African woman and man in hide cloaks kneeling together at the shore, their hands joined over a string of white shell beads, with a basket, a bone, and loose shells on the ground and a dusk sea behind them.

images.title: Family
images.description_1: A grandmother, her daughter, and a newborn share one fur under a cliff on a winter night. The young mother sleeps. The grandmother keeps watch while horses move through the snow.
images.description_2: Studies of fossil teeth show that in the later Ice Age, many more people lived long enough to become grandparents. Grandparents helped raise children and passed on what they knew. Some scientists think that this was one of the strengths of our species.
images.alt: Oil painting of a white-haired grandmother, a sleeping young mother, and a sleeping newborn wrapped together in a fur blanket beside a small fire under a cliff, with horses in the snow behind them.

images.title: Care
images.description_1: A young man brings water in an ostrich eggshell to the elder who once told the band its stories. The elder cannot travel far now. The band does not leave him behind.
images.description_2: Fossils from many sites show people who lived for years with injuries or illness that they could not have survived alone. At Diepkloof Rock Shelter in South Africa, people carried water in engraved ostrich eggshells about 60,000 years ago.
images.alt: Oil painting of a young African man handing an engraved ostrich eggshell flask to a white-bearded elder in a rock shelter, with a child watching, an abalone shell of food, a walking staff, red handprints on the wall, a small fire, and a moonlit rocky beach beyond.

images.title: Art
images.description_1: By the light of a stone lamp, a mother presses her hand to the cave wall and blows red ochre around it through a hollow bone. Her child watches the mark appear.
images.description_2: Hand stencils are among the oldest cave art in the world. One in El Castillo Cave, Spain, is more than 37,000 years old. Some stencils in European caves are so small that they belong to children. A lamp carved from sandstone, like this one, was found in Lascaux Cave, France.
images.alt: Oil painting of an Ice Age woman in a fur parka blowing red ochre through a bone tube around her hand on a cave wall covered with hand stencils, a horse, and a bison, while a small child watches in wonder beside a sandstone oil lamp.

images.title: Friendship
images.description_1: Two friends gather mussels at low tide, and a wave knocks one of them into a tide pool. His best friend laughs too hard to help, then pulls him out.
images.description_2: At Pinnacle Point, on the south coast of South Africa, people collected shellfish about 164,000 years ago. It is some of the oldest evidence of humans who lived from the sea. Low tide was a time to work, to gather food, and to be together.
images.alt: Oil painting of two laughing young African men on a rocky shore at sunset, one sitting soaked in a tide pool and the other pulling him up by the hands, with a hide bag of mussels, pink seaweed, breaking surf, and a cave in the cliff behind them.

images.title: Collaboration
images.description_1: Before the storm, a family builds a winter house from mammoth bones: jawbones for the walls, tusks for the roof, and hides on top. Each person has a job, and the grandmother tells them where things go.
images.description_2: At Mezhyrich, in Ukraine, people built round houses from the bones of dozens of mammoths about 15,000 years ago. Each house needed tons of bone, carefully stacked. No one could build one alone.
images.alt: Painting of an Ice Age family building a round shelter of stacked mammoth jawbones and skulls in the snow, two men raising a curved tusk arch, a woman spreading a hide, a boy pulling a cord, a grandmother pointing, a girl carrying a bone, a small fire, and mammoths on the horizon.

images.title: Endurance
images.description_1: A family walks into a blizzard. The strong carry the children and support the elders, and a young woman protects the embers of their last fire with her own body.
images.description_2: At the coldest point of the last Ice Age, about 20,000 years ago, ice covered much of northern Europe. People moved south and kept going. When a band moved camp, it carried everything: the children, the elders, the tools, and sometimes the fire itself. We are here because they did not leave anyone behind.
images.alt: Painting of seven Ice Age people in fur parkas walking through a blizzard toward the viewer, a young woman holding glowing embers in a birch-bark container, a man carrying a child on his back, a young man supporting a white-haired woman with a staff, a boy carrying a hide bundle, and an older woman holding an infant.
